utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. Alexis Demirdjian for the Prosecution, with Indah Susanti, our case manager, and Ivana Martinovic, our legal intern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to inform the parties, and the record will reflect, that Judge Mindua will leave court at 10.00. His presence is necessary in the judgement rendering hearing in the Prlic case. Thank you. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are just a couple of preliminary matters which I want to deal with before the witness is brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: First of all, last Thursday Mr. Stringer circulated an e-mail with respect to a document which was marked for identification with Witness Christian Nielsen. This was Exhibit P369. The translation has now been revised. There is a missing title. So we would ask that at this time the MFI be lifted and that the document be fully admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Comment from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the MFI status may be lifted, Mr. Registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: On -- on another matter which arises from your decision of the 29th of January, Your Honours, it was in relation to the very next witness. It's the decision granting our 92 ter motion for Witness GH-110, Milorad Vojnovic, and other witnesses. In your decision at paragraph 8 you highlighted the fact that 13 documents were being tendered publicly, whereas in e-court they were designated as confidential and you asked the Prosecution to look into the matter. We can inform the parties that these documents do not require any protective measures and that the matter has been fix in the e-court. So the designation as confidential has been removed as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And that's all the matters that stem from that decision. And yesterday, one last thing, we did send a notification to the parties that in the 92 ter package of the next witness, we found two documents that have already been admitted under different 65 ter numbers. They are duplicates. So essentially we notified that 65 ter 638 and 676 are being withdrawn from the 92 ter package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would suggest for the next witness that the Trial Chamber warns him pursuant to the Rule 90 of the Rules. It is the Rule 90(E) of the Rules. Given the nature of his testimony and given some -- some other circumstances that could arise from his testimony and consequences for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's the first I hear of it so let me take a look here. According to the Rule, the witness may object to making any statement and the Trial Chamber may compel him, so I suspect that we should defer until the matter arises. We have no indication that the witness will object to answering questions, at least not from the testimony in previous cases that we have seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I may briefly, Mr. President. I've consulted with Mr. Zivanovic before coming to court. Warnings of this nature are routine in other cases, it hasn't happened so far yet in this case, but if there is a potential for the witness to incriminate himself, it's best that a warning be given as a blanket matter at the beginning of the testimony because, as you know, there is no lawyer present to advise him in respect of specific questions whether they might incriminate. So the practice in other cases has been a blanket warning at the beginning where there is a potential for the witness to incriminate himself. And that's clearly the case when you look at the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If the Prosecution says there is in -- in the Prosecution's opinion there is no risk and you say there is, do I have to conclude, then, that there will be in your cross-examination? So the moment we give him this warning would be at the beginning of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that the warning should be given at the beginning of the examination-in-chief because any of the answers that are given, even to the Prosecution's questions, could lead to liability not just before this Court but before other courts. In fact, the statement itself -- the 92 ter statement itself contains information that is incriminating to the witness. He's present during crimes. And that being the case he -- even on the basis of the 92 ter statement, there is a potential for incrimination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, very briefly, I quickly checked in the prior cases and just for your information such a warning was never issued to the witness, so it hasn't been the practice at least in relation to this witness in the two cases he's testified; that is, the Mrksic case and the Seselj case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness. First of all, do you understand me -- do you hear me, sorry, in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Witness, sorry, could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Witness, could you please tell us your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Milorad Vojnovic. I was born on the 15th of October, 1945, in the village of Gorica, the municipality of Sipovo, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Now could you please read the solemn declaration the Court Usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Vojnovic, let me also tell you that if an answer to any of the questions would incriminate you, you have the right to say so and to refuse to answer. If you do that, the Trial Chamber will consider whether it is justified or not and eventually compel you or admit your refusal. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Demirdjian, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct to say that you are a retired colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am a retired colonel of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that you have given statements and have testified in prior cases in relation to events which took place in Eastern Slavonia in late 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I testified twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to be specific, it is correct that you testified in the Mrksic case and the Seselj case?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In December last year, you were met by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and you signed a new statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this statement incorporated portions of your previous statements and testimonies; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we bring up 65 ter 6374, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vojnovic, in a moment you will see on the screen a document appear on the right screen before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Colonel, do you see the document before you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what we see here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I see here a witness statement given by Witness Milorad Vojnovic. I see the father's name, ethnic origin, religion, date of birth, occupation, former occupation, languages spoken, the dates of the interview, interviewer, interpreter, names of all persons present during interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And do you see your signature at the bottom of this page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: For the record this statement is of the 11th and 12th of December, 2012. Could we go to the next page, please. Page 2. Let's go to the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Colonel, do you see your initials at the bottom of this page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is it correct that you have initialed every page of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can we go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: On the top of this page, is that your signature under the witness acknowledgment?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Vojnovic, yesterday were you given an opportunity to review your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that you noted some minor errors which you wished to clarify?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. So we will go through these corrections now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we go to page 3 in both the English and the B/C/S versions and zoom onto paragraph 5, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, do you see that at the end of this paragraph it states here that you retired on the 1st of January, 2001. Did you wish to make a correction there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I retired on the 1st January 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to page 4 in both versions please and zoom onto paragraph 8. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 you discuss the war diary of the Guards Motorised Brigade, and I think that you wish to bring to our attention an issue relating to the terminology used here with respect to the Guards Motorised Brigade. Can you clarify that for us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I felt that the term "war diary of the Guards Motorised Brigade" covered my unit, the 18th Motorised Brigade, and the war diary of the Guards Motorised Brigade is a different document. I did not have access to the war diary of the Guards Motorised Brigade. I only had access to the war diary of my own, the 80th Motorised Brigade. So that was what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now when you gave a statement in the Seselj case in 2008, were you given at that time access to the Guards Motorised Brigade's war diary?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not have access to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And were you given an opportunity to look at it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now with respect to the term that we see here in B/C/S, "motorizovane brigade garde," is that the term that is usually used for what was known as the gmtbr or Mr. Mrksic's unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The wrong term was used. You -- you don't have the letter that should be here in front, gmtbr, G standing for "guards," so the term was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So in B/C/S the term is not correct. In English we see Guards Motorised Brigade. How would you say it in your language? How would the term be? The full --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: "Guardiska motorizovana brigada [phoen]," "Guards Motorised Brigade." And my brigade was the 80th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to page 20 in the English version and page 21 in the B/C/S version. And let's focus on paragraph 52 please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Here I think you had a clarification to make with respect to the second sentence which reads: "I do not remember if I issued any specific orders to my officers who stayed there before I left for the briefing with Mrksic." Could you tell the Court what was the clarification you wished to make here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: At that time when I was there, none of my commanding officers or officers were present there. A captain arrived later. I think his name was Vukic. I warned him about the man in the hangar. He was the highest-ranking officer there, Vukasinovic, and I said, "Do you see the highest-ranking officer there?" He said, "Yes." I said, "That's Major Vukasinovic," and I said, "You should talk to him and ask him if he needed any assistance whatsoever." Later on he told me that he had spoken to Vukasinovic once asking him if he needed any assistance and Vukasinovic said he did not. After about half an hour or thereabouts, Vukic went back and spoke to Major Vukasinovic again asking him if he needed assistance. Again he said he did not. And then Vukic asked him if they were free to go, and Vukasinovic said they were and they could indeed leave. I spoke about this encounter with Captain Vukic already and it was not recorded here, although it had been recorded in the previous statements I had made. I cannot account for this omission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. We'll come back to the events. We'll just take a look at the statement for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to page 22 in the B/C/S version, which is page 21 in the English version, and zoom in -- zoom onto paragraph 55, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Colonel, I think you had a comment with respect to the first sentence where you said that, "... Dragi Vukosavljevic told me that the situation was complex." I think it is the term "zamrsena" in B/C/S which you wanted to clarify?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a mistranslation in the B/C/S. The term that was used in the B/C/S version was not actually correct. The term that is used would be more something like "confused," and in fact what we wanted to convey was that the situation was complex and difficult. So the term "zamrsena" is not really correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And I don't know if the record shows what would be the appropriate term in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the term would be "slozena," "complex," "nejasna," "unclear." Because you could not really see all the possibility outcomes of the situation because it was so complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can I take you now to paragraph 60 which in the English version is at page 23. In the B/C/S version it's page 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in this paragraph you're dealing with your encounters with Kameni and you explained that after the Ovcara incident search groups were formed to gather broken weapons and I think you wanted to fix the word "broken."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's actually the term that is used in B/C/S was not correct, what we meant by "broken" was "damaged" or "left behind."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And there is one last correction which is at paragraph 89.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's page 32 both in the English and in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, here we see a reference to Colonel Milan Belic. And it says here that he's of the 1st Proletarian Guards Mechanised Division. I believe you wanted to correct something here too.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Belic was not from the 1st Proletarian Guards Mechanised Division, he was actually a general -- I think it was actually General Milan Delic who was from the 1st Proletarian Guards Mechanised Division. Colonel Milan Belic was from a brigade that was deployed in Ilok. So this is not the correct designation of his unit. He was not the same man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And at the time did you -- did you know Colonel Belic at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I saw Colonel Belic once in Ilok. I don't know him all that well so I can't really tell you anything about it. I don't know where he served. I just saw him once. I knew that he was the commanding officer in Ilok and that he was performing his tasks there. I knew that he had organised life and work in Ilok after the operations there in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Colonel Vojnovic, thank you for these corrections. Now other than these modifications that we just made, is the statement accurate to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you the same questions in the courtroom today would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, I would tender 65 ter 6374, the amalgamated statement, as well as the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I do not object to the tendering to amalgamated statement but I have objections as to some of the exhibits from the package, Rule 92 ter package. I have many objections as to these exhibits and I would ask the Trial Chamber to give me some time to give details for my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, again, this is the first we hear of it, and this is a matter I would say for cross-examination. If there are any issues about either -- I don't know. I don't know what the issues are, really, but I think this is a matter for cross-examination. As usual, the 92 ter package should be admitted in whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, I would say that many of these particular documents have not been -- have not any nexus with -- with the witness statement. For example, many of these documents are first time shown to the witness and he didn't issue these documents. He didn't -- these documents does not concern -- did not concern either him or his unit. And in this sense I would object to -- to admission of these documents. I would specify each of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is not the appropriate time. If -- the Trial Chamber already ruled that the documents that were attached to this statement were relevant and appropriate for admission. Again, if Mr. Zivanovic has an objection with respect to any aspects of the document, he can raise them in cross-examination and cross-examine the witness on that basis. But the witness has already stated to the Trial Chamber that what is in the statement is accurate to the best of his recollections. The comment are there with respect to each document. He has comitted himself to them to the extent that he commented on them on this statement. So at this stage, again, we would say that it is part of the package and you have already ruled on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll try to take a decision after the first break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I believe there is no objection to the statement so that one can be admitted already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's fine. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement 65 ter document 6374 shall be assigned Exhibit P1981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Colonel, as I indicated to you now we will get into some additional questions relating to the topics in your statement. Since your statement is admitted, we don't need to go in all the details. So I'll ask you very specific questions. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now first to put us in context a little bit, Colonel, would you say that your unit, the 80th Motorised Brigade, arrived what would be the latter part of the Vukovar operations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Almost towards the end of the Vukovar operation is the time when the unit arrived in that area. I think that part of my unit did arrive around the 6th or the 7th to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And that would be, just to be clear, the month of? When you say the 6th or the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. November, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it is an admitted fact in this case - and this is adjudicated fact 108 for the record - that your brigade came under Mile Mrksic's command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The majority, or rather, the whole brigade was under his command. I was his subordinate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And it is also an admitted fact in this case, Mr. Vojnovic - and this is adjudicated fact 109 for the record - that your Chief of Staff was Rade Danilovic and that your chief of security was Dragi Vukosavljevic. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just some clarification. It is said "admitted fact." I don't know, is it adjudicated fact or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I used the word "admitted" for the witness. But it is an adjudicated, yes, adjudicated fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So, Colonel, could you confirm that the two names that I mentioned, Mr. Danilovic and Vukosavljevic were part of your staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Rade Danilovic was Chief of Staff and Dragi Vukosavljevic was security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: With respect to Vukosavljevic, could you tell us to whom he reported in his line of work?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: In his professional sense he reported or submitted reports to the security organ of the Operations Group South.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And could you tell the Court a little bit about the structure of your brigade, like what type of soldiers did you have at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: In my brigade I have only a handful of active duty members. Mostly it was made up of the reserve force and there were some active duty officers. Later, active duty officers were assigned commands of the units where -- but the majority of the brigade were members of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how did your brigade compared to the brigade commanded by Mile Mrksic, the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to compare. The other one had a huge core of active duty members and it was even reinforced with officers from other places like, for example, from Belgrade as opposed to us who were mainly composed of reserve forces and reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did your brigade have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Demirdjian. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Colonel Vojnovic, I was going to ask you: Did your brigade have a military police unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what was its strength?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this unit was a company. It has two military police platoons and one transport platoon. One of those military police platoons was subordinated to -- to the Guards Brigade in advance. So let's say that there were some 30-odd people in that company. And the level of manning was not 100 per cent. One of the platoons had to go and join another unit, leaving one transport per platoon and one military police platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how about the Guards Motorised Brigade. Did they have military police unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They had larger military police units. Whether they had one or two of them. But, anyway, they did have military police. It was a bigger unit and better equipped than the units that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now you said that in your case you had one company. Are you aware of what was the level of the military police unit of the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. But it was definitely stronger than ours and it was better equipped both in terms of equipment and skills and professional levels, et cetera. The formations are not equal in or -- all units. The Guards Brigade had a better MP unit and it was a kind of elite unit which was better equipped and better trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now in your statement at paragraph 12, for the record, you mention that your units did not directly participate in combat operations but rather they were there to keep control of liberated areas. And you also explain that, however, some of your resubordinated units were used by other brigades for combat. So can you explain this a little bit to the Trial Chamber how this worked when your unit, the 80th Motorised Brigade, arrives in Vukovar? What -- what you are assigned with?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: My unit was given a task of controlling the area, the territory, to provide security for the population and logistical support wherever it was possible for the population. Elements of the units that were resubordinated to the Guards Brigade were probably involved in combat operation, but we did not command them and they were not subordinated to us until their operations in Vukovar were completed and at that point they returned to our unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Vojnovic, are you familiar with the contents of the war diary of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we play 65 ter 556 which is at tab 46. And this is part of the 92 ter package. And can we go to page 2 in both versions, both in English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now on both versions, do you see at the top the words war diary, 80 mtbr, 9 November to 19 November 1991. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I see it clearly. But as for the handwritten part, I can't see it clearly. But as I recall I know that the 2nd Motorised Battalion had gone to Tovarnik. And the 3rd Battalion was also deployed in the Vukovar area and the same applies to the PVO artillery battalion as well as the 105-millimetre artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. So we see the first few entries. We see 1 mtb, 2 mtb and 3 mtb. What does "mtb" stand for?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: A motorised battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I notice an error in the English translation. It is written as "motorised brigade." We will fix that to reflect that it's "motorised battalion." Now are you able to see the deployment here for 2nd Motorised Battalion, or would you like us to zoom in a little bit on that part of the screen if that would help you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is that a little bit better?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was deployed, provided security for the village of Tovarnik, the 2nd mtb. And the 1st mtb was engaged in the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade but neither of them was subordinated to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. So here we see that the 2nd and the 3rd Battalions are engaged in security. So is that what you were telling us earlier in terms of the assignments that were given to your battalions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell us maybe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber who made the entries in this diary?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, typically and based on their experience that would have been done by an operation organ, but I think that a reserve captain was the one who kept most of the diary. I can't remember his name. I think he was from either Raca or Topola. He was a good lad. He was an engineer, a reserve officer, and he kept this diary in a responsible way and to the best of his ability.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And during the time that we see here between the 9th and the 19th of November, 1991, where was this diary kept?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: At the brigade command HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 12 you say that your command, HQ, was in Negoslavci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I would ask you to situate that on an aerial image.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we play 65 ter 6282, which is at tab 63, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Colonel, in a minute I will ask you to mark this aerial image on the screen with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we could zoom in a little bit -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Colonel, were you given an opportunity to look at this aerial image before you came to court?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't. My command post upon arrival to Negoslavci designated by the Colonel Mrksic was located on the left-hand side towards Vukovar. That's the last house. So it would be approximately somewhere here, the last house or one-before-last, if I remember correctly, viewing in the direction of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The usher will hand you a pen that is connected to the board and you can mark with that one.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is where the house was. Somewhere here. The last one on the left-hand side viewed towards Vukovar. I didn't use the pen maybe properly, but it's on the left-hand side of the road. It was an old abandoned house. It had a big room inside and that is where we were stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you write the number 80 next to the dot that you just marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And are you able to roughly indicate to us where the OG South command post was in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the command post of the OG South was somewhere beyond this intersection. A little bit downwards, maybe the second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you put the letter OG in that area.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And was that on the main street or on one of the side streets?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: It was on the main street, as was my command post and so was the command post of the OG South. My command post was closest to Vukovar, some 3 or 4 kilometres away. And the same distance is between Negoslavci and Vukovar as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now roughly could you tell us what is the distance between both command posts, the 80th and the OG?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll rephrase. Can you tell us what was the distance between your command post of the 80th Motorised Brigade and the command post of the OG South on that street?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it wasn't more than 500 metres, 300 to 500 metres maximum. They were both on the main street but the OG South command post was in a more urbanised area in a better house that provided better conditions for the work of the command as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. We will talk later this morning about the events at Ovcara but since we have the image on the screen here, are you able to see on the right side of the screen the location marked as Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: From memory, I know it's been 20 years, but are you able to give us an approximate -- approximately the distance between Ovcara and the command post of the OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not more than 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May the record reflect that Judge Mindua left the courtroom and that we sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And are you able to show us on this image what was the road that you took from Ovcara to get to the OG South command post that afternoon on the 20th of November? And you don't have to be precise. I know it's a very general image.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a kind of road leading from the OG command post downwards towards Ovcara. There is another road from Sotin in the upper part that leads to Ovcara from the top part. So you can reach it from -- you can reach Ovcara from two or three directions. One from Negoslavci, then if you go towards Vukovar, Jakubovaci. There are some dirt roads as well which are not plotted in this map leading towards Jakubovac and other places, but they were used as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That should suffice for our purposes, Your Honours. May I tender this marked image?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1982. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Colonel, I will move to a different topic. It is at paragraph 7 of your statement that you discuss the issue of volunteers and you indicate here that volunteers were not subordinated to your brigade. However, you mentioned that individuals from Serbia, and you give the area of Sumadija, tried to join. They were removed after a few days because their main interest was looting. And I'd like you to clarify for the Trial Chamber, how did you come to learn about their presence in the area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Up until then there were no volunteers in my brigade but following the liberation of Vukovar, some informal groups appeared in order to offer assistance to the citizens of Vukovar in terms of repair works and other things. Actually, their intention was not to join the unit and place themselves under the control of this unit but they just were interested in what they can gain from that and what can -- they can loot. I cannot tell you exactly where these groups came, but most of them came from Sumadija and they numbered some seven or eight people each. My commander told me that we should expect such groups to arrive. And when it -- that happened we ordered a bus and sent them back first to Sremska Mitrovica and then to their places of origin. We didn't provide transportation -- actually, we didn't send them back. We just provided transportation and they went back on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I would like now to move to the period of time where you discuss the fall of Vukovar and this is as of paragraph 31 of your statement. And you explain here that with the fall of Vukovar your brigade was involved in evacuating certain groups from the area, and you mention one group led by Filip Karaula. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a group of the Croatian Armed Forces, so the HDZ. They were about a hundred men strong. They fought quite fiercely at Mitnica against our forces. In the end they were surrounded and they were forced to surrender. This unit was headed by I think his first name was Filip but his last name was Karaula. So it was about a hundred men strong, this unit. We were tasked with securing this group and in order to be able to do this job properly, I assigned only officers to secure them until the next day when they were transferred to Sremska Mitrovica, probably to some kind of a prison. And there were no problems. We didn't have any problems with those people that we eventually handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you a few questions about this event. First of all, who informed you or who assigned you to this task of receiving this group led by Karaula?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know specifically who gave me that task, but we did receive this task. I knew that we were supposed to secure this group and to escort it to Sremska Mitrovica. I was probably not in the HQ at the time when the order was relayed to us, but I accept this command as an order that had come from the Operations Group South. I did not question it. We simply did the job professionally in a soldierly manner without any incidents, and we were able to transfer the whole group to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And before going to Sremska Mitrovica -- well, did this group go directly from Mitnica to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers were transported directly to Sremska Mitrovica and the group was secured by Vezmarovic. He commanded the military police platoon in my unit. There were some other COs from my brigade but I can't recall their names. Some other commanding officers. But I don't know, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to this topic, I would like you to look again at the war diary of your brigade and hopefully the handwriting will be clear enough for you to comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It is again 65 ter 556 at tab 46. And I would ask that we go to page 14 in both versions. Yes. In the English version we can zoom in on the bottom part of the page, and in the B/C/S version I would ask that we zoom in on the middle part of the page around the area which says 1400 hours or 1410. Yes. Thank you. Can we actually scroll to the right a little bit. A little bit more for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: First of all, Colonel, do you see that little note on the very far right side of the page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But it's illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we zoom in on it, please. A little bit more -- yeah, that square right there. Maybe zoom out one notch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I can read it correctly, it says "Vukic is" -- no, "Vukovar was liberated. At 1200 hours the fighting stopped."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can zoom back out and -- yeah, go back to the 1410 area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now we see that this is a little bit here higher on the page. On the left-hand side we see the date. On the B/C/S version it says the 18th of November. And the entry is at 1410. Now do you see the entry at 1410 here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I can see the number but I cannot really read what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is it possible to zoom a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are you able to see the sentence that begins with: "All brigade officers and some of the the ic, zv, and VP soldiers were ordered to form up." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't see it really.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the time code on your screen? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: 1410. Yes. Yes, now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can you see the sentence here which says that: "All went to the Ovcara farm in Vukovar with the task of getting a camp established to receive prisoners, members of the ZNG and Croatian MUP from the Mitnica sector." Do you see that area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't see it really.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we zoom a little bit on the centre of that screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It's right next to 1410. It's that one dash there. It's a paragraph, five lines.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at it, yes. An order came for all brigade officers the line up and that the 1st Company -- and the 1st Military Police Platoon -- well, I know what happened. This order came in. The officers went there. They were lined up at Ovcara. Then they were given the task to secure the prisoners from Mitnica to make sure that they came to no harm and that they should be handed over at Sremska Mitrovica. That's what it probably says, but I cannot really read it and I already explained about the group. It was Filip Karaula and his unit. They fought at Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And maybe it's better then we go off of your memory in that case. Do you remember the reason for the selection of the Ovcara hangar as the -- or the Ovcara farm, sorry, for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the only facility in that area that was suitable for the accommodation of the prisoners. We knew that they would not be there long. It was isolated. It was -- it had a roof, and it was really the only facility, the only building where you could actually put a large number of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Let me move on now to the events of the -- well, actually, before I do that, you did tell us earlier that you had no problems with this group, the Karaula group?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. Once we took over we had no problems. They behaved very properly. They were told not to try anything and that if any of them would try anything that there would be dire consequences. They did not try to fight back, offer any resistance, or escape. And the commander of the unit, Filip Karaula, was told about all that and they acquiesced. They were not beaten or mistreated in any way, they spent the night in the hangar, and the next day they moved to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you aware of where exactly in Sremska Mitrovica they were transferred to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were moved directly to the prison or to a barracks. I do know that they were taken to Sremska Mitrovica. I heard later that they had been put in prison but I did not check so I can't really tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. So I will move to the events of the 20th of November. In your statement as of paragraph 36 onwards, you explained the events with great detail. And you -- you explain at paragraph 37 that you -- when you arrived at Ovcara on that day, you saw people coming off buses and being beaten and hit. Now, at the time under whose responsibility or area of responsibility was the village of Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Sotin visiting a unit that was part of my brigade, and I spent some time there with the men. I can't really remember the time but it was still daylight when I headed towards the command post. And on route, I got this idea that I should go to Ovcara to visit the commander of the light artillery battalion of the anti-aircraft artillery, Captain Marcek. When I reached his command post, the house where he was stationed, he was there to see me and to report to me, as is proper. And suddenly I saw some buses come in and the buses moved towards the Ovcara hangar. I didn't really know where the buses had come from, who was driving them. We were not aware of any tasks of that sort and I did not wait for Marcek to complete his report. I went straight there to see what was going on. I saw two or three buses that were already parked there. Some buses were already leaving and some people were getting off the buses. I couldn't really tell who they were, prisoners or what. And then in front of the hangar there was about 10 or 15 soldiers, most of them from the Territorial Defence, lined up. Territorial Defence, yes. And the men had to run the gauntlet. They were hit, punched, cursed, and they knew each other. They knew each other's names. I tried to protect those men whichever way I could. I tried to defend them. I tried to prevent those people from harming them, from beating them, if indeed they were prisoners. But some of those people actually said, "Why are you doing this? These are not your prisoners. You have nothing to do with them. They are our prisoners." But regardless of this unpleasant situation, I really tried to protect these men as much as I could and I exposed myself to some unpleasantness. Marcek also came at that point in time. He had been waiting for me and he came there and he helped me. In the end those men entered the hangar and I followed them. I saw that there were a large group of soldiers there. Well, soldiers, what I mean is actually prisoners. Some of them were in military uniform. Some had military uniforms or parts of military uniforms or hospital gowns paired with military boots, all kinds of clothes. I couldn't really identify them. But there was a rope on the -- in the hangar and that's where they were separated into groups. There were -- there were some machinery on the left-hand side. It was probably some kind of a barn or something. So we were there and I observed the situation without knowing what was actually going on. There were about 30 or 40 members of the Territorial Defence there, and I remarked -- two of them, I saw two of them in particular, because they were energetic. They had an air of command around them. But that was the first time that I saw them. One of them was Stanko Vujanovic as I was to learn later, and the other one was Miomir Vujo. And indeed it turned out that they were in charge there. And when --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can I stop you for a second because you gave us a lot of information and I want to go through this bit by bit. My original question was whose area of responsibility was this -- this Ovcara farm located in, and you told us a minute ago that you were coming to visit a Jan Marcek who was stationed there. Can you clarify this, about the area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me explain. Let me just first finish my previous answer and then I will address the issue of the area of responsibility. Marcek joined me and we were able to establish some sort of an order there. And I entered the hangar, spoke to Major Vukasinovic who was standing there right in the middle. He was a very tall man. He was surrounded by a group of men. I couldn't tell who they were, but they were in clean standard issue JNA uniforms. I asked him who these people were, where they had come from, and he said that those were the prisoners from the hospital. That was the first time that I heard about it. I saw him there. In the meantime, I don't know how it happened but my captain, Captain Vukic, joined me. Somebody must have let him know about what was going on. He was a reserve captain. He came with a group of perhaps a squad, about five or six soldiers. Somebody must have told him that I was in danger there and they were dispatched to join me. And I was about to leave, because I had to go and attend the briefing with Mrksic and so I told Captain Vukic, I appointed Major Vukasinovic to him, and I said, "You should ask him if he needs any assistance," because the situation was really complex. It was not clear. And Vukic told me later that he had approached Major Vukasinovic asking him, "Do you need any assistance? My commanding officer had instructed me to approach you." And he said, "No, you can go there. You can go, leave." He did not leave but he observed the situation in the hangar for about an hour. And again, he approached Major Vukasinovic about an hour later, again asking him if he needed any assistance. And Major Vukasinovic told him, "I don't need any assistance. You are free to go." So now, as for the area of responsibility, Marcek was there at the command post because command post had been already determined. It was part of his sector. It was also the area of responsibility of my brigade, part of it. But all the command posts that were there -- well, since there was no organised resistance, there was no fighting because Vukovar had been liberated, what might happen was some commando raids, and the people were still at the command post to guard the relevant axes and defend the area against any such raids. There were no people, civilians, left there except for maybe just a few that were in co-op. But let me just explain one thing: It is quite clear how areas of responsibility are assigned. My superior officer will assign my area of responsibility to me and it is only my superior officer that can enter my area of responsibility without seeking my approval. He can do whatever he wants because he is the commanding officer, the superior officer, and he assumes responsibility for that. All the other officers, all the other personnel, in accordance with the rules of service must report to me. And then we have to co-ordinate our operations to prevent any friendly fire incidents and so on. So in this case the person who assigned the area of responsibility to me also gave himself the right to enter the area of responsibility without my approval. They -- he could do that without asking me because I could not either allow or prohibit him from entering the area of responsibility because my area of responsibility was part of the area of responsibility of the Operations Group South. We secured our area, we controlled and monitored those specific locations and axes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you indicated to us that Major Vukasinovic was in the hangar and in your statement you clarify that Vukasinovic was from the Guards Brigade - and this is at paragraph 46 - and that he was Major Sljivancanin's deputy then. Can you tell the Court what was the status of operative group south on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Where -- this was the largest group and the commander of the OG South commanded the OG South and all the units in the area that were supposed to be subordinate to him. He issued orders to all the units specifying the activities that had to be carried out. As regards Major Vukasinovic, he was the deputy security chief in OG South, so he was Major Sljivancanin's deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. You also told us earlier two names, Stanko Vujanovic and Miroljub Vujovic, you mention them at paragraph 42 of your statement. And then you also say that Vukasinovic in particular seemed to be the Commander-In-Chief. Could you tell the Court how you came to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I saw both of them. That was the first time that I saw them. Their body language, the way they moved, the aggressive manner in which they behaved, they were both armed -- well, I can't really say whether they issued any orders but -- but they did talk to each other and to other soldiers, and I could see that the other Territorial Defence members who were there obeyed them. Stanko was really tall. He wore a cap and he strode around the hangar as did Miroljub. Miroljub was a bit smaller. He wore a green sweater. But they issued orders. I can't really tell you what kind of orders they were. I did not listen to what they were saying. I did not really pay that much attention. But I could see that they seemed to be in charge and that others obeyed them. So that was my conclusion. And in the end it did, indeed, turn out that they did have some units in Leva Supoderica, and this was both confirmed both by this Tribunal and in the court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And before we take the break, let me wrap up on this topic. You mentioned later in paragraph 61 of your statement that before the Guards Motorised Brigade departed for Belgrade, you had a meeting with Sljivancanin and he introduced you to Vujanovic and Vujovic. And I would like to ask you to tell the Court whether after this introduction you had the occasion to see Vujovic and Vujanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Before they left, there was a room in Velepromet. I cannot tell you what kind of a room it was, but there was a meeting with quite a few members of the Territorial Defence. About 30 or 40 of us were in that room. I don't know why I was there but I must have been told that I should be there. I saw Sljivancanin there and I also saw Stanko and the other guy and some other people I can't really remember now, but Sljivancanin told them who I was and that I would be there and that I would be the commander of the city. That's when I first -- first saw them. I did not encounter them all that often. Miroljub came to the command once or twice to make some arrangements, some things had to be solved, but they did not really come there often. They had their own HQ where they would all gather. I think it was in an area that was called Holivud. It was a residential area. A very nice area. That's where they gathered. And when the Guards Brigade left I encountered Kameni several times. He came to the brigade command of his own accord, but the others they did not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I notice the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Demirdjian. Mr. Witness, this is our first break. We will come back at 11.00. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I verified during the break with respect to the 92 ter package of this witness, and we have an e-mail from the 4th of January where the Defence stated that they will take no position and would make no submissions with respect to this package. So again, I would say it defeats the purpose of Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, that is something that one can read in our 28 January --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- in which we did find that the tendered statements and associated exhibits are relevant and have probative value and are appropriate for admission pursuant to Rule 89(C) and 92 ter. And as the conditions set forth in Rule 92 ter have now been fulfilled, the documents will be admitted and marked. I suppose the Registrar will circulate the memo for the numbering. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like us to pick up on what we are talking about before the break and this was with respect to Miroljub Vujovic and the fact that he was introduced to you again by Major Sljivancanin after the fall of Vukovar. I'd like to ask you, after the events at Ovcara, how would you qualify your relationship with Miroljub Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, Miroljub Vujovic was an energetic individual. He enjoyed recognition and esteem among his co-fighters, but he wanted to have a last say in everything and to be everywhere at all times, including the setting up of a draft officer and the authorities and everything. He made a lot of promises but he failed to keep them. I had an opportunity to make two or three agreements with him in order for seeking assistance from volunteers in the hygiene and other measures, removal of dead bodies, and repair of roads. He even promised a number of soldiers to be at a designated time. But they were not there, so I concluded that he was the person that I couldn't rely upon and that was particular the case at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now I'll move on to the topic of the -- the briefing after you left Ovcara the afternoon of the 20th of November. This was something that you mention as of paragraph 54 of your statement, and you say here that you reported to Mrksic about the maltreatment of prisoners which you had personally seen and you say here that Mrksic replied, "Don't talk about it." Now when you briefed Mrksic about the situation, were you speaking to him alone or are there other officers around?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to the operations south command, there was this briefing room and it was nearly packed with people. The meeting was close to the end and everybody was standing up. I reported and I apologised for being late. I told them that I had come from the situation where I saw a commotion. I didn't know what was happening there, how the prisoners were being treated, and I even didn't know what kind of prisoners they were, whether they were wounded or what kind of intervention they needed. They were being treated in an inappropriate manner. They were being pushed around, insulted, belittled, and everything else that was inappropriate to which he responded, "Don't talk to me about this." I was simply stunned by that, by his answer. I thought at first that he didn't understand me and that he wasn't aware of what was going on there. When the meeting finished we all went outside and he and I established a contact again, and I asked him, "Colonel, what am I going to do about the situation?" And he said, "Why do you need to be there?" Which indicated to me that it wasn't my place to go there, that this operation was carried out without me, without my officers. We didn't know anything about it. We were not engaged. I just happened to be there and I happened to see it. If that hadn't been the case, I would not have been possibly in the situation that I was. I understood that his response was a well-intentioned one when he said, "You needn't go there" and "you needn't become yourself involved in a situation that you didn't know anything about." Later on we heard different stories. I understand that this kind of operation had to be done in a speedy way, that it was not necessary for everyone to know about it, and that it was done on a need-to-know basis for only a certain and specific number of officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now at the time with respect to the gmtbr, you explained to us earlier today in comparison to your unit that it was better equipped, better manned, what was the state of affairs with regards to the Guards Motorised Brigade and the manpower available to Mrksic on that day? Could you tell us a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the moment I cannot tell you exactly what the Guards Brigade tasks were in other sectors and axes. However, in the area of the hangar and Ovcara I saw a number of their officers belonging to the Guards Brigade, starting from the Chief of Staff, that is to say, Mrksic's deputy, to security officers, to Vukasinovic -- actually, I didn't see Vukasinovic but I heard that Captain Karanfilov, one of the security organs, was deployed there and he was also a member of the Guards Brigade staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I am going to move now to a different topic, Colonel Vojnovic, and this is one which deals with the establishment of town commands which you deal with at paragraph 22 onwards of your statement. Now you say here that after the fall of Vukovar and the events that you just described, you were appointed as town commander, and you explain that you were ordered to establish local town commands in your area. Now here you said this was a verbal order of Milan Mrksic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: That is right. Prior to their departure, during the last-but-one briefing in Negoslavci, Mrksic said that the 80th Brigade accepted the tasks and obligations that had by that time been undertaken by Operations Group South in the area, that I was appointed town commander of Vukovar and Borovo Naselje. I don't remember seeing a written order to that effect but it probably did arrive at a later stage. All the obligations that the OG South and the Guards Brigade had were to be taken over by us. In the meantime, an order came through the military district command and the OG South command to my brigade, and I can say that I am proud of my officers and soldiers who made a considerable contribution to the overall situation in Vukovar by their conduct and their manner of carrying out tasks, although they suffered a number of casualties. This is probably out of context but I wanted to mention it. So command posts were designated and our task was to decide command posts in each and every village where it was possible and where people were still residing, and as a result and based on my order the command post was set up in Negoslavci, Ovcara, Jakubovac, Sotin, Pinjaci [phoen], and some over villages which I cannot recall at the moment. And that's what we did. These commands posts were manned mainly by officers who were capable of exerting control of the area and to prevent incursions by terrorist groups. These command posts and these unit commanders received sort of instructions or guidelines, either through conversations or in writing. Anyway, our task was -- or their task was to secure vital facilities in those places such as waterworks, transformer stations, power lines, et cetera, in order to make it possible for certain patrols to be set up in certain places, to organise some labour that needed to be done; in a word, to keep law and order in those places by preventing looting, plundering, and taking away equipment from these villages, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 12 of your statement you mention a report which you signed, and perhaps it would be useful to display it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 731 at tab 24. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now this is the 29th of November, and we see the stamp of the command of the 80th Brigade. At the time, Colonel, could you tell us on the 29th of November who was the 80th Motorised Brigade subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, we were resubordinated directly to the command of the 1st Military District because our brigade was the largest one in the area which is the situation following the departure of the Guards Motorised Brigade. We became subordinated to the 1st Military District Command. I don't know for how long this lasted but it was definitely about a month, more or less. I don't think that's important at this juncture. After that we were emerged -- merged with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of the unit and for the benefit of the interpreters asked to speak more slowly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Colonel, the interpreters are asking us if we could slow down a bit so they can keep up with you, and they are asking if you could repeat the last sentence where you said: "Don't think that it's important at this juncture." And you mention a unit and a commander, I believe. If you could repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that initially on or around the 29th for a month or so a unit and command that had been subordinated directly to the 1st Military District Command. After that period, and I don't know exactly when, as a command we were resubordinated to the 1st Proletarian Mechanised Division whose commander was General Mico Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for repeating that. And looking at this document, we see here that the title is: "State of combat morale in the units of the 80th mtbr." And I'd like to take your attention to the second paragraph. Do you see the paragraph which begins with: "Following the liberation of Vukovar ..."?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that: [As read] "Following the liberation of Vukovar, the brigade command, as the town command, was tasked with securing a military authorities and to create conditions for establishing civilian authorities and to have all the health services, [indiscernible] services, other services running and operating, as well as to prevent criminal offences." This was done because they wanted to make it possible for the command of the 80th Brigade to become engaged in its primary role which was to secure the area of responsibility to control the area within the zone, to train officers and soldiers who were member of this unit, and these were its combat tasks and thereby the town command were to relieve the brigade from the burden of carrying out these specific obligations. For that purpose, the command post of the town command was designated and it wasn't a part of the brigade nor was it situated in the Vukovar barracks. It was in a detached location. I don't know exactly where but I went to see them there. All these units such as the town command, the hospital, the police company that was established, and some other units that remained there, were under the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade. And in that manner the brigade was able to operate and the town command made it possible for all these other activities that I mentioned earlier to be carried out, of course, with our approval and with our assistance. They used to visit us on a daily basis in order to report to us what they had done, how far they had progressed, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now you just told us a moment ago that the command post of the town command was detached from the brigade command. Could you perhaps explain to us what does this command post look like? How was it manned? How was it organised?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The town command was detached and it was not in the same place as the brigade command. It was in the neighbourhood of the city of Vukovar, at the point of entry to Vukovar from Negoslavci in a house. I know that it was close to the house of a well known singer from Serbia. I don't remember her name. Her sister is called Goca and she's a folk singer from Serbia. Anyway, she had a house there. And there were two or three officers posted there, there was one vehicle, and about two soldiers who acted a security officers. They co-ordinated all these village command posts and provided assistance to people and organised things as much as they were able to do. But that was the situation that prevailed until I left Vukovar on the 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. You just told us that in the house there were two or three officers posted there. Is that all in terms of the town command? Is that all in terms of manning or structure?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the entire composition. There were no other officers or soldiers there. Those were the people who manned it. And they were not even members of our unit. By virtue of some order they had been sent there by the 1st Military District Command, but while they were there they were subordinated to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now going back to this second paragraph here, there is a part of the sentence that says that the town command is tasked with ensuring the conditions for the revival and the establishment of the civilian government, judiciary, health, economy, et cetera. Could you perhaps tell the Trial Chamber and describe to them what was the situation with respect to the civilian government when you took up your role as town commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: When I assumed the duty of town commander and other responsibilities, there was nothing there. Nothing was working. Nobody could go anywhere to seek help. Of course, since at that time the military authorities were operational, everything had to go through the command. Since the brigade command did not intend to stay there and exert its authority any longer, they wished to establish these institutions as soon as possible that would provide for civilian governance of Vukovar. I don't remember the exact date. I believe that I received instructions from someone on how to organise these matters, and for that purpose we called a meeting at Velepromet where we intended to establish civilian authorities in the city of Vukovar. Rajko Bibic, maybe he's not called Rajko but that's what he was called, was among them. He used to be the manager of the co-operative, if that is correct, and he was one of the better educated people, and I met him. These authorities had to have between 14 and 16 members. Now I was guided by the idea to have people who were capable of carrying out these duties, so a list of 14 or 16 individuals was made. I showed the list to Rajko. And on the list there were two men that he told me that we should not mention their names at any cost because he feared the reaction of other people, some 50 or 60 of them who were present on the premises. So I gave it to him and he read the list of the names. Whether he omitted these two questionable names or read them in a low voice, I don't know, but anyway the people who were on the list were elected to form a government, the Executive Committee, and other structures. It was Rajko Bibic who took over these tasks from that point. I believe that the first president of the municipality was Dr. Visic, I don't recall his first name, but Dr. Visic at any rate. And I can tell you that even the venue that they have chosen were quickly made operational for administrative work. They carried out the necessary organisational work. But I wasn't too much privy to what they did. I used to visit them occasionally, asking them whether they required any help. Every day they worked on these issues and I know that certain people, for example, those who used to work at Vuteks were managers of that factory, and I know that in Borovo Naselje it was Markovic who was appointed. But before that, I issued an order as commander of the military authorities and in accordance with the consultations of the people who were versed in these problems, I appointed these people; for example, Radan Jovica in Vuteks.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the second name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, an order was announced on TV - I don't know where it had come from - that Markovic was appointed the manager of Borovo. At the time he was a deputy or whatever. Anyway, in view of everything I described, things were set in motion, and after that they started moving towards the villages. These village command posts were going out of operation and even during the military authority we tried to do something and for that purpose we re-established the water-supply and we made sure for everyone who was starving to come twice to the barracks a day to receive food. We established a transportation service between Vukovar and Belgrade, et cetera. Of course the problems we faced were huge, but there were improvements on a daily basis, shops were being opened and the town was being cleaned up and put into order, particularly the barracks which was the hub of the whole operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Colonel Vojnovic, can I ask you very briefly to explain to us -- you just explained to us the situation with the civilian authorities. There is also a mention in your report here to the judiciary. Could you briefly explain to the Court what was the status when you took over as town commander?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: When I came to the command post, I was not aware of any judiciary because there was no such thing in the brigade. Some extra judiciary tasks, political issues, they were dealt with by our morale organ.
