But investigations, an organised judiciary, there was no such thing at the time and, indeed, throughout the time when I was there in Vukovar in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we go to the last page in both versions, that's page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S. Just go to the bottom of that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is a report that was drafted by you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my signature indeed. And -- yes, it is true that the brigade command and the battalion command that we ordered our soldiers not to move their positions and that they could not leave their positions without the approval and also there is this order from the 1st Military District that some units would be disbanded after 45 days. If I as a commander had some problems in this regard, I know that an order was issued or a communique was issued by the command of the 1st Military District that the soldiers would be rotated every 45 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Colonel, Colonel, I apologise. I don't want to interrupt you, but I would ask that you would focus on the question and you have confirmed that this was a report that was drafted by your unit. That is all I was asking you. And I apologise for interrupting you, but we need to focus on the questions, please. You mentioned elsewhere in your report and you just told us a minute ago that after you established the town commands in Vukovar, then other villages followed, and town commands were established there, too. And at paragraph 22 you say: "My duties were to cease once local government representatives were elected." Could you explain to the Court when in your -- well, in your knowledge, were civilian authorities established in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, I can't be specific about the date and the time. But once the government was in place, the Executive Council and the government in Vukovar, they assumed more and more duties and we assisted them as much as we could and focused more on the military tasks, training, and also repairing the equipment and weapons in that area. I don't remember when it was. There was a certain period of time that elapsed. Well, some things were perhaps set in motion right at the beginning, but some were set in motion later. So it must have been a certain period of time because the government did not have the premises. They did not have the basic prerequisites. They could not really do their job. There must have been some kind of an advisory role, some kind of guidance that was given to them. I don't remember whether that was in December or January. I really don't know the specific time, but sometime in late December or early January. That might have been the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when did the 80th Motorised Brigade leave the area of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The 80th Brigade left Vukovar on the 13th of January, but some of the officers and some of the elements of the command remained, and I left the area together with those units in Kragujevac. I went back to Vukovar seven days later to report to my duty because I had my duties as the town commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You explain at paragraph 26 of your statement that while you were town commander, you had no contacts with the government of the SAO SBZS and that you considered that to be not to be a normal situation. Could you tell the Court why you considered that not to be a normal situation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really was not in contact with the government and I don't know how it was established at the time. I know that there were huge problems and that there were many things to be dealt with in the Vukovar area. Now, I, myself, was not in contact with them. But on one occasion - I don't know when that was - Rajko Bibic told me that he had attended a meeting somewhere and that he had presented some views as to how things should be done. But I did not really have any details and I can't recall what he was saying. I knew that he had gone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, later in your statement you discuss one of the reports which was drafted by the town commander of Ilok, Colonel Milan Belic. This is at paragraph 89 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And perhaps we could display it on the screen. It's Exhibit P371 at tab 32. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you see here that this is a report that we showed you back in December from the town command of Ilok, and in your statement here you say that the document shows the dissatisfaction of the JNA with the government because the government had appointed people who were loyal rather than people who were educated, and you were aware of this situation at the time. Could you tell us how did -- how did this situation in Ilok compare with the situation in your area?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as regards -- well, in comparison with Vukovar, Ilok was a smaller town and it was much easier to establish control and to do one's job there, and yet some problems emerged. They had the same kind of problems that we had. Our problems were bigger because Vukovar was the epicenter, so to speak, of that area. Everybody was looking at it. It was in the centre of attention. It was written up in the media and so on. But the people who were in the Vukovar area, they had come from various places. Not only the Territorial Defence detachments but there were some independent individuals, volunteers. There were commanders who did not report to anyone, and if you had four or five soldiers you called yourself a commander and that man would strut around the town followed by his soldiers calling himself a commander. It was very difficult to co-ordinate anything with them and to work with them at all, particularly because we didn't know those people. I got to know those people who appeared to be in charge, Stanko, Miroljub, and Kameni, and others, indeed, but there were other people that nobody knew. You would have people enter a house, set up their HQ with just a handful of soldiers, and nobody knew how they operated, how they worked side by side, and it was a very big problem. Very much present in Vukovar, to a lesser extent in Ilok. People would move out -- move into the houses and take stuff out. It was like a conveyer belt. Some people would take stuff out, others would be waiting to move in and take stuff in. And it took a while, it took some time, and you had to talk to people. You had to exercise command in order to re-establish order. And -- but that's a normal process. And the same kind of thing happened in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to deal now with my last topic which is the departure of the Guards Motorised Brigade in November. Now, you explained this at paragraph 78 of your statement that the gmtbr left around the 25th of November and it is also an admitted fact - an adjudicated fact in our case, this is 112 - that when the gmtbr leaves Vukovar that the Operative Group South ceases to exist. Is that a correct statement of the facts?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: When the operational group or, rather, the Guards Brigade pulled out of this area, I think it was in the period between the 25th and the 27th, the Operational Group South ceased to exist. The command of the 80th Brigade assumed all the duties that had been exercised by the OG South in that area all the way down to the Vuka river, because all the -- the OG South covered that area. And to the north of us further away from the Vuka river, it was the 12th Corps, the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Finally you explain at paragraph 69 of your statement that before he left Vukovar Mrksic ordered you to prepare and to accommodate a team of investigators who were coming to look into what happened at Ovcara. Now, first, I would like to ask you: Was this a verbal or a written order from Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Mrksic gave me that order at a meeting, at a briefing, at his command post in Negoslavci. He said to prepare a room, that a team of investigating judges and investigators, lawyers, judges, and so on, would come and that they would spend some time there and would conduct proceedings, investigate the events in the area. Of course, the emphasis was to be on the events in Ovcara. I did not have a room that I could set aside for them. I found a classroom in the command building and I made preparations as much as I could given the circumstances, but the team of investigators never reported to me, never came, and later on I think that there was a written order to me instructing me to make those preparations for them, to confirm what Mrksic had told me orally. Well, I actually never saw them. They never came. They never reported to us. I don't know. They may have come but we never saw them, and they never came to us for assistance. Oh, now, yes, I remember. Of all of those who were supposed to come, I only saw the pathologist. He was the captain first-class at that time and later on he was promoted to general, Dr. Stankovic. And I assisted him as much as I could at Ciglana where he carried out the postmortems on the bodies, but I didn't ask him any questions. I don't know whether he was accompanied by anyone else but he was the only one that I actually saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could you just clarify for us, where is this Ciglana.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a building. It's actually brick works. That's where construction materials, bricks, and so on, are made. I am not even sure whether it was the Ciglana brick works. But that's where I was waiting for him. I think that's where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this completes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. But before I start my cross-examination, I would just -- oh yeah, okay, transcript is running. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Vojnovic. My name is Zoran Zivanovic and I am representing Mr. Hadzic in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Good day to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vojnovic, let me just first to ask you to clarify if you can. I have gone through your statement, in particular paragraph 4, that you are a highly educated military professional. In paragraph 5 you state your educational background. But could you please clear up some military terms that have been used in the course of your testimony and were also used in your statement that was admitted into evidence. First, I would like you to explain to us the term "resubordination." What does it entail? How is that different from "subordination"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's just a turn of phrase. Subordination -- to subordinate a unit. For instance, my command was subordinated to the command of the Operational Group South or an element of my brigade. But in some cases, it is not the entire unit or a battalion or just two battalions from my brigade may be resubordinated. So I don't really see a difference between the two terms, in any substantive terms. So you shouldn't really be confused by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then explain it like this: Before you arrive into the Vukovar area, I think that your brigade was subordinated to a different unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. Before I arrived, no. But once I came to the Vukovar area, then it was subordinated to the OG South.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me -- so until your arrival in the Vukovar area, your brigade was not subordinated to anyone, then?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Before the arrival in the Vukovar area, it was part of the Kragujevac Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, it was subordinated to the Kragujevac Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So can we then say that resubordination is an act whereby you get a new superior command - let me just finish - so resubordination is an act whereby you get a new superior command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, well, you could say that. You could interpret it in that way because until our arrival in Vukovar, until we became part of the OG South, we had been subordinated to the Kragujevac Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we looked at several documents and you, yourself, also looked at them, including the war diary of your unit and of the Guards Motorised Brigade. You were also shown the operational log of your unit, and I would like to ask you this: If you can explain, what kind of data are entered into the war diary?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the war diary contains the key tasks during the day; for instance, any movements of the unit, transfers of the unit, any extraordinary events, incidents, any woundings or casualties or traffic accidents, training drills - for instance, shooting practice, and so on - and all the other information that is very important for the unit, any briefings, but not at the lowest level, not at the company level but probably at the brigade level, also meetings that were held at battalion level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The war diary, does it contain entries specifying the most important combat operations that were carried out during the day?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you the diary of the Guards Motorised Brigade. That's document 357 from the Prosecution's list. Let us look at it because I need you to clarify some things for us. Well, you know that your unit also kept a war diary. Could you please tell us whose names are entered here at the cover of the war diary, the first page? You will see it here.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Major Gojkovic, he was from OG South, and Major Trifunovic. The two of them were charged with maintaining the war diary. So, for instance, if one of them was absent then the other one would make entries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please move on to the second page of this war diary. Here right at the beginning you see the date and the time when this war diary first -- was first started to be kept.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I can see that there are four columns. The first column is where you entered the place, date, and time.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please clarify this for me: Is this the place, date, and time of the event in question?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The second column has the heading the description of the event.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The third column contains the names of the people who actually made the entries. I can see that here we see the name of Major Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So he entered this information. And the fourth column you can see that it's -- the heading is "Remarks," so it's mostly who was notified about the events. You can see here in -- "S notified," that would mean Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now we will not be going through this date by date, but would this be the model, the usual format for the war diaries?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the universal format that was used by all the units at tactical level but also from the brigade up and from the brigade down. This was the universal format that was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And it seems to me that it governs by the instructions of the staff commands?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was adopted from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to this we saw a document which is called an operational diary. Unfortunately, we did not manage to get hold of the diary of the Guards Brigade but we had an opportunity to see the operational diary of your brigade. What I'm interested in at the moment, and I don't need to show you the operational diary, but can you explain the difference between an operational diary and the war log? Which kind of information is entered into one and which information is not entered and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The operational diary contains all the activities that are taking place within a unit and within an area during the entire day. There is no significant difference between this and the war diary, only the focus is more on combats activities and the results of combat activities. Operational diaries are kept by higher level units, starting from the level of corps upwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But if I'm not wrong, your brigade kept an operational diary as well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So that means that the brigade as well --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I said that that was the standard format that was being adopted and applied from the level of brigade upwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And this operational diary format -- so let's look at it after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's document 557 from the Prosecutor's list.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at it anyway. Can we enlarge it a little bit so that you can see. You can see at the top the period that this diary pertains to and here it starts on 9th November, 1991, until the 14th of January. I think the 9th November is the day when this unit arrived in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And the 14th of January is the date when it left Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm not sure whether we went back on the 13th or the 14th. But that was before the Serbian new year. And you know when that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be the 13th of January, then, but for the purposes of my question the date is not so relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please enlarge the Serbian version so that you can read it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Here again we have place, time. The next column is "content," then the next column is the signature of the recipient, and remarks. Now, my impression is that all these columns are identical to war logs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that this is the standard format and that we have the same columns. It depends who kept this diary. Here we have an ordinal number and that is the only difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something in relation to another document, let's say, which provided us with certain information and statements. According to our information, JNA officers had their own notebooks at the time where they noted down certain events and data. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. They had their official notebooks that were certified that had stamps on the backside and in which they entered crucial tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say certified on the backside with a stamp, that would be the stamp of their unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If I am not wrong, the pages of these notebooks were marked in advance, and I think that there was a total of 200 of them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were different notebooks and each page had a number. And at the end, the organ who had issued the notebook would put a signature and a stamp on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And they would indicate the number of pages?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. As I said, from 1- to 200. They would say that this notebook contains 200 pages and would put a stamp in order to verify it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you, yourself, keep such a notebook?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us what did you enter into this notebook?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all the activities that were occurring in the unit starting from the tasks assigned to subordinates, attendance of certain gatherings, the problems that you, yourself, need to solve or in co-ordination with other people. Everything that was pertinent to the unit in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you enter, for example, the tasks that were assigned by an officer to his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But perhaps not in so many details. For example, I would say that so-and-so should carry out so-and-so task without going into specific details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And I assume that this notebook contained also what you received from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me this: What happened with your notebook? Do you still have it or is it some place else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. Really, I don't know. Well, there is a lot of things. You take one notebook, you misplace it, you take a new one. But basically once you fill it, you have to return it. It wasn't a big deal. Usually it was either destroyed or you just never returned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But as a rule once the notebook was filled, to be returned to the issuing command, and then you would get a new one; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you said that sometimes a notebook would be misplaced or lost, did that mean that the person who did that was supposed to report that to you? And I am talking about your subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That should have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever face such a situation? And I specifically mean in this period.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never encountered such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you also never lost your notebook?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I just don't know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if you had handed it over?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot be positive about it, but if you return a notebook then they would set up a commission who would then burn it. If we are talking about a big unit, there may be one or two or more notebooks. If you have a lot of officers then this wouldn't be archived. Then we have this commission again who took care of those notebooks and destroyed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know who set up this commission - for example, if you had received a number of officers from your subordinates [as interpreted] - who set up this commission who was going to destroy or burn those notebooks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was usually done by the Chief of Staff or the operations officer. That would be the person who worked in an office, who would stamp these kind of documents, and that would be then taken out and set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when was this procedure applied? Did it happen immediately after handing over the notebook or did they keep it for a certain time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you wouldn't burn one notebook at a time. You would possibly wait for a year or two to collect a certain number of notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if these notebooks kept by the officers in your units, were they burned?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it is the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Colonel Vojnovic, this is the time for our second break. We come back at 12.45. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought in, may the record show that Doug Stringer has joined the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And I want to say that the record should reflect also that Judge Mindua is present again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vojnovic, I am going to show you now a working notebook that we have, and I would kindly ask you that we look at certain parts of that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Exhibit 27 from our list or, rather, Exhibit 503.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is turned around. We can see the front page or the cover page. Is this the way how this operational notebook looked like, the front page and the back page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here a clause on the number of pages, and it reads: [As read] "This working notebook contains 100 (written out 100 pages numbered 1- to 200) and entered into the list of issued notebooks under the number," and then we have the signature of the officer. My question is: Is this the usual clause that was printed at the end of each notebook?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the standard notebook that all the officers had. Some were larger in size, some were smaller, but this is what is written out in each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at page 2 of this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can see that there are some blanks like reference number, type of confidentiality, and the degree of confidentiality. And we have the user's name, Dragan Vezmanovic. Can you confirm he was a military police company commander in your unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You saw on the last page that there is no reference number for this notebook nor the unit stamp nor the -- the officer's signature, that is, the officer who had issued the notebook. And you also see that the same information is missing from the first page. Can you tell me how it happened that in this specific instance the MP company commander had a notebook that had not been verified and certified in a proper way?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot explain that. All this information should have been there including the number, and all these other blanks should have been filled properly. Most probably, him being a reserve officer, and when he joined the unit, he was given this notebook in the office that issued it, who failed to fill out these blank spaces. I said that all of these blank spaces should have been filled with the appropriate information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is it perhaps possible that this notebook was filled in and the entries made only later?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is filled in in sequential order, page by page and date by day. He might have made some entries in advance, but from experience I know that every day when I come to work, I enter a date and then I make notes that relate to that day. So he should have followed the same procedure. You may add something later. But this should have been done on a daily basis. Everything should have been entered regularly every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I was not clear enough when I asked the question. Is it possible that instead of using his certified workbook, which was filled in and destroyed, was it possible that a different notebook was actually used. When I say "afterwards," I mean after the events at Ovcara --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: -- and all the trials at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- Colonel. Yes, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe the question calls for speculation. Could it be that this was re-transcribed, we don't know, and I'm not sure the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot make any claims as to whether this was possible or not. It shouldn't be possible. If all the entries are made sequentially on the pages, perhaps another notebook could be found where further tasks are entered date after date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the left-hand side of the screen, I see the calendar and I see that the years listed here are 1978, 1979, 1980, 1981; in other words, this notebook dates from a period, a decade at least before the events that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's how it's usually done. In that year a large number of notebooks are purchased, not all of them are used up, and then they are simply issued. These are huge batches and, of course, you cannot procure -- you cannot purchase new ones until you have used up all the ones that you already have, and that's how this happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a notebook of this kind bearing those dates or, rather, this kind of a calendar with those years?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you that really. I am sure that we did not have the actual -- the current calendar years. All you had to do is to enter the exact date and then take it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statements and in the course of your testimony, you mentioned the term "area of responsibility." I would like you to tell me, can you define it? What is it, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is an example of irresponsible behaviour because obviously this person did not return the notebook. This is a minor infraction. He was supposed to give the notebook back to his superior because it is said once you have filled in the notebook, you have to return it. Or perhaps it is a major infraction involving failure to carry out some other type of task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am not sure whether you heard me. I asked you: What is actually an area of responsibility? What is the meaning of the term?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. I see. I understand. Well, this means that each and every unit in a given situation in the theater of war is assigned a section of the territory defined by four points, four facilities or features, and this is then its area of responsibility. This is the area in which this unit must deal with all the problems, must engage in combat, any kind of task that needs to be done in that area of responsibility is for that unit. Brigades are assigned areas of responsibility, and smaller units - battalion and down - they are assigned sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me is there a way regulated by the relevant rules in which this area of responsibility is supposed to be secured?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's up to the command and indeed the commander. It is secured by the deployment of the units. You have to establish control of the territory by deploying your units. Units go out on patrols, sentries are set up, reconnaissance activities are carried out, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me now, what was the area of responsibility of your unit in the period after the liberation or the fall of Vukovar? Whatever you want to call it. So after the 18th of November, 1991, and from that point in time onwards?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really specify all the locations because you get it on the map. It is plotted onto a map which is part of the commander's decision. It is drawn in felt-tip pens, and also you have the command post of the superior command, of your command, of the subordinate commands, the adjacent units, and so on. Everything is defined there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me then whether your area of responsibility, the area of responsibility of the 80th Brigade, included Ovcara among other locations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you if the area of responsibility of the 80th Motorised Brigade included Ovcara as in the village of Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was there and it was assigned to my unit, but later on it was taken away from my unit, from me, because the area of responsibility is defined by the superior commander. And in line with the rules, no one can enter your area of responsibility without your express approval and knowledge with the exception of the superior commander. That would be the person who actually assigned the area to you. In this case, that was the commander of the operational area south. They or he could enter each and every sector he wanted and to set up a position there and I, as a commander, could not do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to clarify this. You say that this unit -- this area was given to you and then taken away from you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The moment they entered the Ovcara, the hangar sector with their own commanding officers, with their own soldiers, they took that position and that was from that moment on their sector and they were responsible for it. They assumed all the responsibility. They had to perform all the duties, all the obligations, and also all the risks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just analyse this a bit further. You said that the commander or whoever it was that assigned this area of responsibility to you could enter the area at will without anyone's approval.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But the way I understand it, the commander never entered this area of responsibility. In fact, some other people did.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but his officers were there. His Chief of Staff was there, his security officer was there. His assistant for morale was there as well. So that doesn't mean that he's not responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell us that all those officers or soldiers from the superior command could enter the area of responsibility without notifying you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. Only superior officers could enter the area. Not just anyone from the brigade command. It was part of the OG South command that was located there. They were my superior command and there was some really high-ranking and responsible commanders; as I said, the Chief of Staff, the security officer, the assistants and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, can you please give us their names?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff was Lieutenant-Colonel Miodrag Panic, he was later promoted to general; the security chief was -- in fact, the deputy security chief was the one that I saw there, Vukasinovic, Major Ljubisa Vukasinovic; and there was a colonel who was in charge of morale, I don't know his name, but I knew that he was there. I went back with the colonel. Now, I don't know whether he was the one or not. I couldn't really tell you. Well, I saw later on -- or, rather, I didn't see him, but I knew that he was there, Captain First-Class Karanfilov [phoen], and there were some other people there. I am sure that the people I have named were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you mind repeating the name of that captain first-class.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Karanfilov. I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw those officers there, you also saw a mass of civilians. I understand why you felt that those officers were entitled to enter into your area of responsibility, but why did you allow the civilians to enter? You said that some of them were even armed. They were not personnel of the OG South of your superior command.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: This entire operation was led by some officers from OG South and they were present there, so the highest-ranking officers with the greatest deal of responsibility and authority. And I could not ask any questions because they were either -- they either outranked me or were at the same rank as I did. They brought those people in. I didn't know who they were. I said that there were people dressed in all kinds of clothes, mix and match, military shirts or shoes or hospital gowns paired with military boots, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I said that there were civilians there, I did not mean the prisoners. I meant the other civilians, the ones that you said attacked you, caused commotion and that they mistreated the prisoners, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we have a reference for the witness ever saying that there were civilians there? I don't recall him using the word "civilians" with respect to the non-JNA persons who were present when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He has described. That's right. I'll clarify it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You saw some people who mistreated the prisoners. You described in your statement how they had to run the gauntlet. You described the situation in the hangar. Can you now tell us your opinion? Well, I'm now asking you about the people who actually mistreated the prisoners. Did you consider them to be members of the unit that was part of the OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see the officers from the OG South until I entered the hangar, and men who lined up in front of the hangar wore uniforms and they appeared to me to be members of the Territorial Defence. The civilians were getting off the buses and they were passing through this gauntlet, actually. I saw the civilians enter the hangar. And as I said, they had all kinds of clothes, military and civilian. So it was a mix and match situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to hear from you whether you considered them to be civilians or members of the units that had accompanied the officers that you saw there on the site?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I did not consider them to be civilians. They were people in uniform carrying arms standing in front of the hangar. I don't know how they came to be there, whether they accompanied anyone or what. They were just there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely why I'm asking you this. You, as the commander, and those people entered your area of responsibility. You see those people there. You see what they are doing. Did you do anything to have them removed because you didn't know who they belonged to. They wore uniforms, that is a fact, but it didn't mean a lot in any way and they were rank-and-file soldiers and you are an officer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I took measures to prevent them from beating and abusing the prisoners. Together with my officers I protected myself and the two soldiers, that was just as they were getting in. I entered the hangar and I saw an officer there from the OG South. He was really the high-ranking officer -- the highest ranking officer in the security service of the OG South, and I asked him, "Who are these people?" He said, "Those were the people from the hospital." And I couldn't do much more than that. And I really couldn't ask him any further questions because I didn't know what his task was, what these people were doing, and he told me then that those people had come from the hospital. There were other officers from the command with him including the Chief of Staff, so really, I mean, I didn't see the Chief of Staff because he was standing by the hangar to the side. And there was another officer, assistant commander, standing by the side lines just observing the things. I -- when I came there, I risked my own life and limb to protect the people because I felt it was the right thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The officer that you saw inside the hangar, was his name Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What rank did he have?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: He was a major at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And he was subordinated to Major Sljivancanin, I think?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think so too. Anyway, he was part of the OG South security detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you don't know who was the chief of security of OG South?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Except for asking him where those people had come from, and I suppose you meant the prisoners, did you talk with Vukasinovic about anything else?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask him who the people who were beating the prisoners were?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, because I saw those people. He was inside but I don't know if he, himself, saw it or not and how long he stayed inside. But most of the people were already inside when I arrived and when I saw them. Perhaps an additional one or two buses arrived. One of them was already leaving. So the people from the bus ran the gauntlet, and once this process of entering the hangar was over I went inside. I saw a group of soldiers, I saw the prisoners, I told you how they were dressed. Some were sitting on the side. Some were standing in groups and talking amongst themselves. And then I asked Vukasinovic the question I asked, and he gave me the answer I told you. I was happy to see him there and I was happy that he was aware of what was going on and what his task was, and I thought it wasn't my place to ask him any further questions. All I wanted to know was where those people had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify a bit the answer that you have given me. You said that he was inside and that you don't know if the prisoners were beaten or not.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't ask him that. I only asked him where those people had come from. I didn't say the word "prisoners" because I didn't know the definition of who these people were. I just asked who are these people and he said the prisoners from the hospital. That's the first time that I saw those people, those prisoners being maltreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm interested in the following: Why didn't you tell him about what you had seen? You had seen these people being beaten up and maltreated by some people in uniforms or partial uniforms. Why didn't you inform him or why didn't you ask him, "Who are theses people? Who are beating people" outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask him. I only informed my commander. When I arrived, when the soldiers entered the hangar, I left. I went to see my commander and gave him the account of what I had seen. And I told him that people were being beaten up, were maltreated, et cetera, while they were entering the hangar and it was about 10 or 15 metres before they reached the door, and they were beaten with everything they could get hold of. They were kicked and punched and beaten up with rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you tell Vukasinovic anything about this? He -- it took some time for you to reach him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to deny that I never asked him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Colonel, would you please not speak while Mr. Zivanovic is still speaking and preferably have a little pause between the two of you so that the interpreters can follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said today that you and Vukasinovic were inside the hangar and that you saw a group of people dressed in M77 military uniforms. Can you tell us something about M77 uniforms? What does that mean, M77?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, before we go to that answer, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: When I interfered I interrupted the witness, and he answered your previous -- or he started answering your previous question why he didn't tell Vukasinovic anything about what was happening outside, and the witness started to answer saying: "Well, I'm not going to deny that I never asked him ..." And then I stopped him. So now I would ask you, Colonel, to continue what you were -- what you planned to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I wanted to say was that I wasn't sure if I told him that the soldiers outside were being maltreated. I cannot say that for sure. But I don't believe that under such circumstances I failed to mention this to me [as interpreted]. And, on the other hand, I am sure he did indeed know about that, as well as his Chief of Staff who was standing outside the hangar and whom I saw only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were not sure about telling him that the soldiers outside the hangar were being maltreated. Is that what you wanted to say? I know that you said that in Serbian and that's how it was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, not soldiers. The prisoners. The people who were getting off the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you're not sure, did you ask him - but probably you don't remember the answer that he'd given you if you asked him.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I did not debate this issue with him for a long time. I only asked him, "Who are these people and where do they come from?" That's verbatim what I asked him. And he replied, "These are the people from the hospital." I stayed there for a while longer and then I went to the OG South command post where I briefed my superior about what I had seen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Weren't you interested why these people were beating the prisoners. Why didn't you ask them why they were doing that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I saw that they knew each other, that they were addressing each other by name, and that they were even using derogatory names in addressing each other. And then when I saw Vukasinovic standing inside, I said that there are people there without any insignia whatsoever, without any caps. I realise that that was all. I had nothing else to do that [as interpreted]. And I decided to go and report it to my commander. And that is when he told me what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, you said that you saw Vukasinovic surrounded by a group of people dressed in M77 uniforms. Can you explain to us what -- the meaning of M77 uniform?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a new type of uniform that was introduced at the time, different from the old one. If you remember, it was manufactured in 1977 for the purposes of the Yugoslav People's Army. For the officers, it was a working uniform. And for ordinary soldiers, it was a dress uniform. And then it turned into an every day regular uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the number 77 indicates the year of manufacture; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I think. The same applies to the weapons, 48 is 1948. You have M-53 and other types of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to put to you your statement or, rather, your testimony given Mrksic case. That was on the 15th of May, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Exhibit 4628 and the number 22 on our list. Let us move to page 22. And then it goes on to page 23 in e-court. That's line 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out in English and you're going to listen to the interpretation. This is your response: [In English] "I saw a group around Vukasinovic. They were wearing regulation uniforms. They were military personnel. I don't know who they were, but mostly they were all without caps and I didn't know those people. They were all wearing our M-77 military uniform. "Q. And can you just assist us what the M-77 military uniform looks like without going into a fashion statement? "A. That was the standard uniform at the time in the Yugoslav People's Army and was olive-drab shirt and pants. There were boots and at the time we -- it was a cap that we called the Tito cap, as well as a wind-jacket. This is what all the senior officers wore, and these particular officers were wearing all of those things." [Interpretation] Do you remember this evidence that you gave?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that this is all correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at Ovcara in the vicinity of the hangar, I think that you saw a couple of buses and you saw the prisoners alighting from the buses. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from these buses, did you see any other vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I saw only one passenger car, Renault 4. It was parked on the side some distance away. And next to it was an officer. He was a thin man, not too tall. He had the rank of colonel. I approached him and asked him what is all this about, what's happening here. Can you help us introduce some order here. He didn't give me any answer at all, just entered his car and left. I didn't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He had a higher rank than you did?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were lieutenant-colonel at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that there is a rule in the military which is part of the rules of service that if an officer is approaching an officer senior in rank, the junior, so to speak, officer should identify himself. Did you do that? Did you tell him your name and what your role there was so that that was your zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember identifying myself, but I saluted him in a military manner and I asked him, "What's happening here?" Now, whether he recognised me and my position, I don't know, but that was the first time that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen him anywhere else at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am not referring only to Vukovar. I mean later.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I was reading reports and following the proceedings. I think a name was mentioned but I don't know what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember what name was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really remember. It's at the tip of my tongue, but I can't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us to the best of your recollection -- well, you were 46 at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether he was older than you were, younger, whether you were of an age? Can you just give us your estimate.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that in addition to being higher than I was in rank that he was also older than I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And he left after a brief encounter, after what you told him. He left in this Renault car?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you don't remember the colour, the paint colour? Do you remember by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I am not sure whether it was red or olive-drab. It was -- I think it was sort of like greenish in colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And were you able to see if he was alone or if he had some kind of escort, another soldier?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw him standing there on his own. Now perhaps there may have been somebody standing a couple of steps away from him or behind him, I don't know. I didn't see anyone at any rate. So he probably was accompanied by somebody. I don't know if he drove the car. He probably was there with somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me if you saw any military vehicles there, such as the various all terrain vehicles, Pinzgauer or Puch or Kampanjola cars?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't see any vehicles there. No, I just saw the buses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason why I am asking you this is because you saw some officers in addition to this colonel. You say that you didn't see some of them but you knew that they were there. I'm assuming that they drove there. I don't suppose that they had come there on the same buses that had brought the prisoners in. So I'm asking you whether you saw any vehicles that they may have used to get there and get back again?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I think about those events I was probably much too concerned about the people, so I didn't really pay much attention to vehicles. But they must have got there somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So can we then conclude that when you were there in front of the hangar and inside the building that the way I understand it you did not tell the colonel and Major Vukasinovic, "What you are you doing in my area of responsibility? Who are these people? Why have you brought them here? What are you doing to them," and so on?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say anything of the sort. I knew who Vukasinovic was, which unit he belonged to. There were some other officers there as well from his command which was superior, and they were -- they outranked me and indeed they outranked him. I assumed that they had a task but I didn't know what the task was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say other officers, you mean Panic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Panic, the Chief of Staff, Karanfilov. Well, there may have been others, although I didn't see them, because I wasn't really trying to see which officers were actually there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that in addition to having to run the gauntlet and abuse, that the documents were taken off the prisoners. Their identity documents.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see where the documents were put?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I think there was some kind of a bag, some kind of a suitcase or something like that where the documents were put. It was an old fashioned bag of this sort. Like a travel bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as an experienced officer, how did you interpret this fact that documents were taken from those people? Was this the usual procedure? Was this how you always treat the prisoners? Or was this a contravention of the rules?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought that the documents would be used to make lists to determine the identity of the people, to simply take their personnel details, so that those documents would be delivered to somebody who would then check their identity. That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you did not find this unusual?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. The fact that documents were taken from these people? No, no. I thought that this was the reason why documents were taken away from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that the day before, if I'm not mistaken, a group of prisoners were also brought to Ovcara and that you secured this group, your personnel from the 80th Brigade, the guards were mostly officers, and that the next day this group was transferred to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether documents were taken from those prisoners, too?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I came to the hangar when they were already lined up, a list had been made, and they were taken away after their identity was checked against this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who made this list?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the group that was taken to Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who made this list. They were brought there. I was told who the commander was - well, I've already told you about that several times - Filip Karaula. He was told how to behave. He said how many of them there were. I don't know whether he made the list. But all we had to do was take receipt of them, so to speak, to secure them overnight, which we did, and the next morning we took them to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not know when the list was made? When they were -- when they arrived there or where it was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was done there or in the sector where they had surrendered. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you don't know that you or any other officers from the 80th Brigade issued any orders to the effect that documents should be taken away from the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at the work notebook. That's 503. That's page 14 of this workbook or operational book. In fact it's page 15, I think. It's 27 -- page 27 and the ERN number ends with 1291. Next page. Yes. That one. No, I'm sorry. I may have misspoke. I probably have the wrong list. I think we'll need the list that's at page 302.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the operational book that we have been discussing and now I am talking about the pagination in the notebook itself, so from pages 49 through - just a moment - 65, you have a list containing the names of a large number of people. And they appear to be the prisoners that you are talking about, the ones that were at Ovcara the day before. Could you please tell me -- well, I see that you have the first name, last name, father's name, and the year of birth listed for each and every prisoner, so I want to know whether you knew or had been told about when this list was made?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. I just know that they were transported where they were supposed to be transported, that everything went smoothly. There were no complaints. And this was probably done by Vezmarovic who actually secured them. He put those names in the notebook because he had to know the identity of the people that he handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he report to you that he did this list?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you inquire about it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. What I wanted to know was whether everything had gone smoothly, and then when he got back he told me that everything was fine and that he was able to hand-over the same number of people that he had initially taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell me who handed over the prisoners to him or to your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Those prisoners were handed over to us from an element of the OG South. This group of prisoners was secured and brought to the hangar by Colonel Nebojsa Pavkovic. He was a colonel at the time. So he brought them there and he told Filip Karaula, "Now it's up to you to obey these people. Do whatever they tell you." And then Pavkovic left.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you actually see Nebojsa Pavkovic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us what you talked about on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't talk about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And how was this hand-over effected if you didn't talk about anything?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were brought to the hangar. I don't know how we received notice that we should go there and take-over those prisoners who were in the hangar. I didn't know who had brought them there until I saw Pavkovic. That was the first time. And that's the only thing he actually said to their commander and he left. He didn't even say hello to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did any of the people in his escort talk about this issue with any of the officers from your unit; for instance, from the military police company or from the securities organ?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't really tell you. I arrived there in the evening. They were already lined up in the hangar. They were standing next to the wall. Then they were allowed to sit down, to have a smoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason why I am asking you this is because you say that Vezmarovic told you that he had handed over the same number of people that had been handed over to him, so it has to be noted down somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I said that Vezmarovic had handed over those people, that he then had come back and reported to me that everything had gone smoothly. And this notebook, which probably belongs to him, I don't know, I can see that he made a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I may have misunderstood you or something else but I'm not going to dwell on this. Well, did Vezmarovic tell you how the hand-over had been effected, whether he left them there in Mitrovica and just turned around and left or whether there was any document there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he just got back and he reported to the brigade command that he had handed over the prisoners, that there had been no problems. An entry was made to that effect and that was the end of it. So -- and he just said that he had handed over the same number of people that had been handed over to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So he did tell you that he had handed over --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, he did not. I learned the number later. I don't know who told me that or how I learned that. But he did not give me the exact figure. He just said that everything had gone smoothly and that he had handed over the same number of people that he had received. I don't know if he was accompanied by any other officers, but as an officer of the military police it was his duty to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You did not ask for any kind of document as proof that this was actually done?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was enough that it was noted in the war diary and it was indeed confirmed at the briefing that Vezmarovic had handed them over. Vezmarovic reported that in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now we're not going to be talking about these prisoners but the prisoners that were brought there on the 20th of November. After you left the hangar, you went to attend a briefing with Mrksic, and you said that, among other things -- well, first, he said that you should not mention that to him at all. And later on he said -- he asked you who had sent you there and why you had gone there at all; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you tell him that you had gone there because it was part of your area of responsibility and that he himself knew that very well because he had assigned it to you in the first place?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: No, because that was not the reason why I went there. I went there from Sotin, from my unit because I wanted to visit an artillery battalion commander who was there in his command post in the village of Ovcara. So that was the only purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood it. But I assumed that you went to see the buses at the hangar precisely to see what was going on, and you probably would not have followed each and every bus anywhere, but you did that because this was your area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: At that time I was really stunned to see the buses because I didn't know why they were there. I wanted to see who those people were and I saw those things that I actually described. I -- I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: Had I gone in a different direction and if I had headed directly to Vukovar from Sotin, I would not have seen this. I would have learned about it only the next day or even some days afterwards, but I had some time on my hands and I wanted to visit this commander because I wanted to have as much information as I could for the briefing with Mrksic and to report to him, and I reported to him about the things that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what I find really strange? I find it really strange that Mrksic asked you what you were doing in Ovcara and he knew very well that Ovcara was part of your area of responsibility and that in a way it was only natural for you to tour your area of responsibility and to keep an eye on what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD VOJNOVIC
utterances.text: What he found strange was the fact that I did not know about the events that were going on. My officers did not know that this thing would happen there and that this task was supposed to be carried out in an organised manner involving as few of other personnel as possible. Only some people -- only a few people were supposed to know, only those who were actually involved, and it was supposed to be kept secret from everybody else including myself and that's why he was asking me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is that time indeed, Mr. Zivanovic. Colonel, this is the end of the hearing of today. We will see you tomorrow morning at 9.00. You are not released as a witness. That means that in the meantime, while you're still on the stand and still a witness, you are not allowed to discuss your testimony with anybody and you cannot talk to any of the parties. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon. Just to -- so that the Chamber is not taken by surprise tomorrow, you may recall that the witness who is currently testifying was switched when difficulties were encountered getting the necessary authorisations for the witness originally intended, and the result of that is that when the current witness has completed his testimony tomorrow, there will not be another witness available then to continue on. We are short this week because of this -- of having to make that switch, and so I thought I would just bring that to the Chamber's attention at this time rather than so you are not caught by surprise tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. That could be a not-to-unlucky coincidence because tomorrow there is a visit -- the Tribunal has a visit from the president of Germany and that gives us perhaps a little more time. So thank you very much for your information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I should probably add that the -- the issue or the problem encountered that prevented the intended witness from coming has still not been resolved, and we are pushing hard to hopefully get that resolved and identifying potential other witnesses who might be able to come instead if it comes to that, but I -- I -- since I'm doing my mea culpas I should just put it all out there for Your Honours at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of May, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 25
